newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Russia sees WTO entry next year, minister signals.
newsitem.headline: Russia sees WTO entry next year, minister signals.

text.p: Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov signalled on Tuesday he expected his country to win admission to the World Trade Organisation by the end of 1997.

Davydov, who is also foreign economic relations minister and Moscow's chief negotiator on WTO entry, was speaking at the first Ministerial Conference of the two-year-old body -- now in discussion with China on membership terms for a decade.

"The integration of Russia into the world economy is an integral idea of the reform process in my country," he told the gathering of ministers and officials from the 128 states already in the organisation.

"In our view, it is impossible to achieve such an aim without becoming a part of the global trading system. That is why we consider our accession to the WTO as an important factor to support our reform."
In the negotiation process, under way since 1993, "we would anticipate that the next year will be a decisive one," Davydov declared.

Under communist rule, Moscow leaders regularly denounced the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), as a grouping of "imperialist powers" focused on exploiting the Third World and declined all contact.

But in contrast to China, which maintains its official commitment to communism, Russia has formally rejected its Soviet past and says it is working to build an economy based on the capitalist, free-market system.

Also unlike Beijing, which insists it must be admitted to the WTO as a developing country on easier terms, Moscow accepts that it will have to come in as a fully-industrialised power with no special conditions.
"Our approach is pragmatic," Davydov said on Tuesday, "We will be ready to start bilateral negotiations on specific terms of our accession in the nearest possible future."
Earlier on Tuesday, a Foreign Ministry spokesman in Beijing said China had done enough in opening its domestic markets to qualify for entry and was being blocked by the West for political reasons.

And in Singapore, a bid by the European Union to launch a new effort to remove barriers to Chinese entry -- also aiming at an accord next year -- failed, with the United States saying Beijing could only come in "on commercially meaningful terms."

Davydov said Moscow expected that Russia's own foreign trade situation would improve once it was in the WTO, whose basic principle of most-favoured-nation (MFN) and rule-based system aim to ensure fair trading among all members.
"Equally, our trading partners would enjoy more stable and predictable conditions for their products in the Russian market," the Russian Deputy Prime Minister said.

"During a short period of time, the Russian trade regime has been liberalised radically," he told the conference. "Russia does not apply quantitative restrictions on imports or other non-tariff measures inconsistent with WTO rules.
"Our import customs tariff is therefore the main instrument of trade regulation. As a result, our foreign trade is very dynamic with an annual average rate of growth of more than 12 percent."
